citations.claim: Oxford-style debates are a competitive format where the winner is determined by audience votes.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1604.03114
Conversational flow in Oxford-style debates
Abstract
Public debates are a common platform for presenting and juxtaposing diverging views on important
issues. In this work we propose a methodology for tracking how ideas flow between participants
throughout a debate. We use this approach in a case study of Oxford-style debates---a competitive
format where the winner is determined by audience votes---and show how the outcome of a debate
depends on aspects of conversational flow. In particular, we find that winners tend to make better use of
a debate's interactive component than losers, by actively pursuing their opponents' points rather than
promoting their own ideas over the course of the conversation.

citations.claim: The paper constructs statistical models to identify dogmatic comments from a Reddit corpus annotated via paid crowdsourcing.
citations.quote:
We explore linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media and construct statistical
models that can identify dogmatic comments. Our model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts, collected
across a diverse set of conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing. We operationalize
key aspects of dogmatism described by existing psychology theories (such as over-confidence), finding
they have predictive power. We also find evidence for new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency
of dogmatic posts to refrain from signaling cognitive processes. When we use our predictive model to
analyze millions of other Reddit posts, we find evidence that suggests dogmatism is a deeper
personality trait, present for dogmatic users across many different domains, and that users who engage
on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves.

citations.claim: The dogmatism paper's data is a corpus of Reddit posts annotated via paid crowdsourcing, unrelated to Snapchat captions.
citations.quote:
We explore linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media and construct statistical
models that can identify dogmatic comments. Our model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts, collected
across a diverse set of conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing. We operationalize
key aspects of dogmatism described by existing psychology theories (such as over-confidence), finding
they have predictive power. We also find evidence for new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency
of dogmatic posts to refrain from signaling cognitive processes. When we use our predictive model to
analyze millions of other Reddit posts, we find evidence that suggests dogmatism is a deeper
personality trait, present for dogmatic users across many different domains, and that users who engage
on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves.

Each dataset variant consists of around 200k training instances and 4,096 validation instances, plus
4,096 test instances. Each training instance consists of an image and a reference caption. At test time,
only the test images are available to the evaluated models. Underlying world models are kept from the
models and are used for later GTD evaluation. For each test instance, we sample ten reference
captions of the same distribution as the training captions to enable the comparison of our proposed
metrics to BLEU and SPICE. We fine-tune our model hyperparameters based on the performance on
the validation set. All reported results are measured on the test split with the parameters yielding the
best validation performance.

documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it

In NMT, words are sometimes dropped from the source or generated repeatedly in the translation. We

citations.claim: The paper experiments with three ways of setting source-word fertility: constant, guided and predicted.
citations.quote:
We experiment with three ways of setting the fertility of the source words: constant, guided, and
predicted. With constant, we set the fertilities of all source words to a fixed integer value INLINEFORM0
. With guided, we train a word aligner based on IBM Model 2 (we used fast_align in our experiments,
BIBREF17 ) and, for each word in the vocabulary, we set the fertilities to the maximal observed value in
the training data (or 1 if no alignment was observed). With the predicted strategy, we train a separate
fertility predictor model using a bi-LSTM tagger. At training time, we provide as supervision the fertility
estimated by fast_align. Since our model works with fertility upper bounds and the word aligner may
miss some word pairs, we found it beneficial to add a constant to this number (1 in our experiments). At
test time, we use the expected fertilities according to our model.

citations.claim: The paper's method mitigates ASR errors by aligning ASR hypotheses with reference transcriptions using adversarial domain adaptation that learns domain-invariant features for the QA model.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Abstract
Spoken question answering (SQA) is challenging due to complex reasoning on top of the spoken
documents. The recent studies have also shown the catastrophic impact of automatic speech
recognition (ASR) errors on SQA. Therefore, this work proposes to mitigate the ASR errors by aligning
the mismatch between ASR hypotheses and their corresponding reference transcriptions. An
adversarial model is applied to this domain adaptation task, which forces the model to learn
domain-invariant features the QA model can effectively utilize in order to improve the SQA results. The
experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, and the results are
better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.

citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Selected passages
In this task, when the machine is given a spoken document, it needs to find the answer of a question
from the spoken document. SQA can be solved by the concatenation of an ASR module and a question
answering module. Given the ASR hypotheses of a spoken document and a question, the question
answering module can output a text answer.
The most intuitive way to evaluate the text answer is to directly compute the Exact Match (EM) and
Macro-averaged F1 scores (F1) between the predicted text answer and the ground-truth text answer.
We used the standard evaluation script from SQuAD BIBREF1 to evaluate the performance.

citations.claim: The proposed model's results are better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Abstract
Spoken question answering (SQA) is challenging due to complex reasoning on top of the spoken
documents. The recent studies have also shown the catastrophic impact of automatic speech
recognition (ASR) errors on SQA. Therefore, this work proposes to mitigate the ASR errors by aligning
the mismatch between ASR hypotheses and their corresponding reference transcriptions. An
adversarial model is applied to this domain adaptation task, which forces the model to learn
domain-invariant features the QA model can effectively utilize in order to improve the SQA results. The
experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, and the results are
better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.

predicted. With constant, we set the fertilities of all source words to a fixed integer value INLINEFORM0

fertility predictor model using a bi-LSTM tagger. At training time, we provide as supervision the fertility

Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a novel neural single document extractive summarization model for long
documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it
outperforms previous work, both extractive and abstractive models, on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and
METEOR scores. We also show that, consistently with our goal, the benefits of our method become
stronger as we apply it to longer documents. Rather surprisingly, an ablation study indicates that the
benefits of our model seem to come exclusively from modeling the local context, even for the longest
documents.

citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Abstract
Spoken question answering (SQA) is challenging due to complex reasoning on top of the spoken
documents. The recent studies have also shown the catastrophic impact of automatic speech
recognition (ASR) errors on SQA. Therefore, this work proposes to mitigate the ASR errors by aligning
the mismatch between ASR hypotheses and their corresponding reference transcriptions. An
adversarial model is applied to this domain adaptation task, which forces the model to learn
domain-invariant features the QA model can effectively utilize in order to improve the SQA results. The
experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, and the results are
better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.

predicted. With constant, we set the fertilities of all source words to a fixed integer value INLINEFORM0

fertility predictor model using a bi-LSTM tagger. At training time, we provide as supervision the fertility
estimated by fast_align. Since our model works with fertility upper bounds and the word aligner may
miss some word pairs, we found it beneficial to add a constant to this number (1 in our experiments). At
test time, we use the expected fertilities according to our model.

Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a novel neural single document extractive summarization model for long
documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it
outperforms previous work, both extractive and abstractive models, on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and
METEOR scores. We also show that, consistently with our goal, the benefits of our method become
stronger as we apply it to longer documents. Rather surprisingly, an ablation study indicates that the
benefits of our model seem to come exclusively from modeling the local context, even for the longest
documents.

Selected passages
We compare the predictions of logistic regression models based on unigram bag-of-words features

features using term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and category-based features by

citations.claim: Given the ASR hypotheses of a spoken document and a question, the question answering module can output a text answer.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Selected passages
In this task, when the machine is given a spoken document, it needs to find the answer of a question
from the spoken document. SQA can be solved by the concatenation of an ASR module and a question
answering module. Given the ASR hypotheses of a spoken document and a question, the question
answering module can output a text answer.
The most intuitive way to evaluate the text answer is to directly compute the Exact Match (EM) and
Macro-averaged F1 scores (F1) between the predicted text answer and the ground-truth text answer.
We used the standard evaluation script from SQuAD BIBREF1 to evaluate the performance.

output.explanation: The Transformer paper says it used beam search with beam size 4 and length penalty α = 0.6, chosen after development-set experimentation, and set maximum inference output length to input length + 50; it reports 28.4 BLEU on WMT 2014 English-to-German. ConvS2S says translations are generated by beam search with beam width 5; it normalizes final-hypothesis log-likelihoods by |y|, and for WMT’14 English-German tunes a length-normalization constant on newstest2015 and normalizes by |y|^α, finding no benefit elsewhere; it reports 25.16 BLEU for ConvS2S (BPE 40K) on WMT’14 English-German. Thus the two systems were decoded with different beam widths and different length-adjustment schemes, including a separately tuned α for ConvS2S, so a BLEU difference is confounded by decoding choices. In addition, ConvS2S uses attention in every decoder layer, so the comparison is not attention versus pure convolution. The BLEU gap alone therefore cannot isolate the architectural effect.

4.1
Static vs. Dynamic Masking
As discussed in Section 2, BERT relies on ran-
domly masking and predicting tokens. The orig-
inal BERT implementation performed masking
once during data preprocessing, resulting in a sin-
gle static mask. To avoid using the same mask for
each training instance in every epoch, training data
was duplicated 10 times so that each sequence is
masked in 10 different ways over the 40 epochs of
training. Thus, each training sequence was seen
with the same mask four times during training.
We compare this strategy with dynamic mask-
ing where we generate the masking pattern every
time we feed a sequence to the model. This be-
comes crucial when pretraining for more steps or
with larger datasets.

output.explanation: The BERT paper's Table 3 lists 'Ours BERTLARGE (Single)' on SQuAD 2.0 with dev EM/F1 78.7/81.9 [S:aa44f0a9f0af#49]. The RoBERTa paper's Table 6 lists single-model dev results without data augmentation, with RoBERTa at 86.5 EM/89.4 F1 on SQuAD 2.0 [S:35327af608ac#58]. Using those own-paper numbers, the differences are 86.5−78.7 = 7.8 EM points and 89.4−81.9 = 7.5 F1 points. The RoBERTa paper itself tabulates BERT-Large at 79.0 EM/81.8 F1, so a comparison using RoBERTa's table would be 7.5 EM and 7.6 F1 points [S:35327af608ac#58]; the small mismatch (78.7/81.9 vs 79.0/81.8) is a cross-paper reporting discrepancy and makes the exact gap slightly uncertain. Causally, no: RoBERTa's recipe changes several things at once—training longer, bigger batches, more data, removing NSP, longer sequences, and dynamic masking [S:35327af608ac#4]—so the BERT-Large-to-RoBERTa gap conflates NSP removal with these other changes. RoBERTa's own base-model comparison shows only a small SQuAD 2.0 F1 difference between its NSP SEGMENT-PAIR model (78.7) and no-NSP FULL-SENTENCES model (79.1) [S:35327af608ac#30], and BERT's own NSP ablation is reported for SQuAD 1.1, not SQuAD 2.0 [S:aa44f0a9f0af#58]. Thus the numbers alone do not identify NSP removal as the cause.

output.answer: EM measures the percentage of predictions that exactly match a gold answer; token-overlap F1 is macro-averaged bag-of-tokens overlap (maximum over gold answers per question, then averaged), and both ignore punctuation and articles. In SQuAD 2.0, abstaining on an unanswerable item scores 1 and a nonempty answer scores 0 for both EM and F1. For test, the no-answer threshold is tuned separately per model on the development set and chosen to maximize development-set F1.

output.explanation: 1606.05250v3.pdf defines Exact Match as the percentage of predictions that exactly match any one of the ground-truth answers [S:fc6fdf3e2afd#60]. It defines the F1 metric by treating prediction and ground truth as bags of tokens, computing their F1, taking the maximum over all gold answers for a question, and averaging over questions [S:fc6fdf3e2afd#61]. Both metrics ignore punctuation and articles [S:fc6fdf3e2afd#60]. 1806.03822v1.pdf states that, for negative examples, abstaining receives a score of 1 and any other response gets 0, for both exact match and F1 [S:919279224fdc#39]. For its test setup, it tunes the no-answer threshold separately for each model on the development set [S:919279224fdc#38] and uses the threshold that maximizes F1 on the development set when evaluating on the test set [S:919279224fdc#38]. SQuAD 2.0 also explicitly follows Rajpurkar et al. (2016) in reporting average exact match and F1 scores [S:919279224fdc#39]. The papers agree on the EM/F1 metric family; SQuAD 2.0 adds the abstention scoring convention and threshold-tuning procedure.

output.answer: ResNet's identity block combines the shortcut with the residual branch by element-wise addition (y = F(x, {Wi}) + x). Inside a DenseNet dense block, each layer receives all preceding feature-maps in that block and concatenates them rather than summing them. A direct consequence is that DenseNet feature-maps remain accessible to all subsequent layers, encouraging feature reuse and more compact models.

The data split is ILSVRC 2012: 1.2M training images, 50,000 validation images, 1,000 classes, with errors reported on the validation set (p.5). The evaluation setup: DenseNet simply replaces the ResNet model with DenseNet-BC while keeping all experiment settings exactly the same as ResNet (p.7), and the authors caution that this means hyperparameters were optimized for ResNets rather than DenseNets (p.7). For the ResNet paper (1512.03385v1), the supplied evidence covers only the ImageNet training/testing protocol — random 224x224 crops, per-pixel mean subtraction, and the standard 10-crop testing used for comparison studies (p.4) — and contains no table or sentence giving the ILSVRC'15 ensemble top-5 error. Because that number is absent, and because even if present an ensemble/test-set result would not be directly comparable to single-model single-crop or 10-crop validation errors on a possibly different split, no like-for-like head-to-head advantage can be established from what is available; the comparison is a setup mismatch (ensemble vs. single model, and validation vs. potentially test-set reporting). The DenseNet paper's own qualitative comparison ('a DenseNet-201 with 20M parameters model yields similar validation error as a 101-layer ResNet with more than 40M parameters', p.7) is a parameter-efficiency statement, not the requested ResNet ensemble number.

citations.claim: DeiT reports 85.2% for its best ImageNet-1k model and compares it with a JFT-300M-pretrained ViT-B at 384 resolution at 84.15%.
citations.quote:
5.2
Distillation
Our distillation method produces a vision transformer that becomes on par
with the best convnets in terms of the trade-off between accuracy and through-
put, see Table 5. Interestingly, the distilled model outperforms its teacher in
terms of the trade-off between accuracy and throughput. Our best model on
ImageNet-1k is 85.2% top-1 accuracy outperforms the best Vit-B model pre-
trained on JFT-300M at resolution 384 (84.15%). For reference, the current state
of the art of 88.55% achieved with extra training data was obtained by the ViT-
H model (600M parameters) trained on JFT-300M at resolution 512. Hereafter
we provide several analysis and observations.

citations.claim: DeiT relies on extensive data augmentation to train with datasets of the same size.
citations.quote:
Data-Augmentation.
Compared to models that integrate more priors (such
as convolutions), transformers require a larger amount of data. Thus, in order
to train with datasets of the same size, we rely on extensive data augmentation.
We evaluate different types of strong data augmentation, with the objective to
reach a data-efﬁcient training regime.
Auto-Augment [11], Rand-Augment
[12], and random erasing [62] im-
prove the results. For the two latter we use the timm [55] customizations, and
after ablation we choose Rand-Augment instead of AutoAugment. Overall our

citations.claim: DeiT describes the class token as a trainable vector appended to the patch tokens before the first layer, passed through the transformer layers, and linearly projected to predict the class.
citations.quote:
The class token
is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the
ﬁrst layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with
a linear layer to predict the class. This class token is inherited from NLP [14],
and departs from the typical pooling layers used in computer vision to predict
the class. The transformer thus process batches of (N + 1) tokens of dimension
D, of which only the class vector is used to predict the output. This architecture
forces the self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and
the class token: at training time the supervision signal comes only from the
class embedding, while the patch tokens are the model’s only variable input.
5

output.explanation: In arXiv:2010.11929v2 (ViT), the class token is a learnable embedding prepended to the sequence of embedded patches; its final encoder state serves as the image representation, and a classification head is attached during both pre-training and fine-tuning [S:09514e334c4e#19]. ViT's appendix says this token's output is transformed into a class prediction by a small MLP with tanh in its single hidden layer [S:09514e334c4e#117]. arXiv:2012.12877v2 (DeiT) summarizes the same class-token mechanism: it is a trainable vector appended before the first transformer layer, passes through the layers, and is linearly projected to predict the class [S:3efc0a7acf39#23]. DeiT further states that this architecture forces self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and the class token, with training supervision coming only from the class embedding [S:3efc0a7acf39#23]. For distillation, DeiT adds a distillation token to the initial embeddings; it is output after the last layer, and its target objective is the distillation component of the loss [S:3efc0a7acf39#29]. Its specific target is the teacher's hard predicted label rather than the true label, so the class branch remains the true-label branch by contrast [S:3efc0a7acf39#28]. At inference, DeiT associates both the class and distillation embeddings with linear classifiers, and its late fusion adds the softmax outputs of the two classifiers to make the prediction [S:3efc0a7acf39#33]. Table 3's class+distillation row is described as corresponding to that late fusion [S:3efc0a7acf39#40]. The papers agree on the class-token description; DeiT adds the distillation token and teacher-target branch. The evidence does not give a more detailed fusion rule than adding the two softmax outputs.

citations.claim: The paper introduces Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) for noisy user-generated social media posts with accompanying images.
citations.quote:
We introduce a new task called Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) for noisy user-generated
data such as tweets or Snapchat captions, which comprise short text with accompanying images. These
social media posts often come in inconsistent or incomplete syntax and lexical notations with very
limited surrounding textual contexts, bringing significant challenges for NER. To this end, we create a
new dataset for MNER called SnapCaptions (Snapchat image-caption pairs submitted to public and
crowd-sourced stories with fully annotated named entities). We then build upon the state-of-the-art
Bi-LSTM word/character based NER models with 1) a deep image network which incorporates relevant
visual context to augment textual information, and 2) a generic modality-attention module which learns
to attenuate irrelevant modalities while amplifying the most informative ones to extract contexts from,

citations.claim: The separate fertility predictor model is implemented using a bi-LSTM tagger.
citations.quote:
We experiment with three ways of setting the fertility of the source words: constant, guided, and
predicted. With constant, we set the fertilities of all source words to a fixed integer value INLINEFORM0
. With guided, we train a word aligner based on IBM Model 2 (we used fast_align in our experiments,
BIBREF17 ) and, for each word in the vocabulary, we set the fertilities to the maximal observed value in
the training data (or 1 if no alignment was observed). With the predicted strategy, we train a separate
fertility predictor model using a bi-LSTM tagger. At training time, we provide as supervision the fertility
estimated by fast_align. Since our model works with fertility upper bounds and the word aligner may
miss some word pairs, we found it beneficial to add a constant to this number (1 in our experiments). At
test time, we use the expected fertilities according to our model.

citations.claim: The paper proposes to mitigate ASR errors in spoken question answering by adversarial domain adaptation.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Abstract
Spoken question answering (SQA) is challenging due to complex reasoning on top of the spoken
documents. The recent studies have also shown the catastrophic impact of automatic speech
recognition (ASR) errors on SQA. Therefore, this work proposes to mitigate the ASR errors by aligning
the mismatch between ASR hypotheses and their corresponding reference transcriptions. An
adversarial model is applied to this domain adaptation task, which forces the model to learn
domain-invariant features the QA model can effectively utilize in order to improve the SQA results. The
experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, and the results are
better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.

citations.claim: The two captioning models experimented with are the Show&Tell model and the LRCN1u model.
citations.quote:
We experiment with two image captioning models: the Show&Tell model BIBREF0 and the LRCN1u
model BIBREF1. Both models follow the basic encoder-decoder architecture design that uses a CNN
encoder to condense the visual information into an image embedding, which in turn conditions an LSTM
decoder to generate a natural language caption. The main difference between the two models is the
way they condition the decoder. The Show&Tell model feeds the image embedding as the “predecessor
word embedding” to the first produced word, while the LRCN1u model concatenates the image features
with the embedded previous word as the input to the sequence model at each time step.

citations.claim: Encoder and decoder components were jointly optimized with cross-entropy sequence loss on the ShapeWorldICE dataset.
citations.quote:
We follow the common practice in image captioning to use a CNN component pretrained on object
detection and fine-tune its parameters on the image captioning task. The encoder and decoder
components are jointly optimized with respect to the standard cross-entropy sequence loss on the
respective ShapeWorldICE dataset. For all our experiments, we train models end-to-end for a fixed
number of 100k iterations with a batch size of 64. We use Adam optimization BIBREF26 with a learning
rate of 0.001. Word embeddings are randomly initialized and jointly trained during the training.

citations.claim: The paper proposes a neural single-document extractive summarization model for long documents and evaluates it on Pubmed and arXiv, outperforming previous extractive and abstractive models on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and METEOR.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1909.08089
Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a novel neural single document extractive summarization model for long
documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it
outperforms previous work, both extractive and abstractive models, on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and
METEOR scores. We also show that, consistently with our goal, the benefits of our method become
stronger as we apply it to longer documents. Rather surprisingly, an ablation study indicates that the
benefits of our model seem to come exclusively from modeling the local context, even for the longest
documents.

citations.claim: The paper fills missing stock-price values caused by weekends and public holidays by approximating the first missing value as (y+x)/2 and repeating the method for all gaps.
citations.quote:
Data Pre-Processing
[s3-p0] Stock prices data collected is not complete understandably because of weekends and public
holidays when the stock market does not function. The missing data is approximated using a simple
technique by Goel BIBREF17 . Stock data usually follows a concave function. So, if the stock value on a
day is x and the next value present is y with some missing in between. The first missing value is
approximated to be (y+x)/2 and the same method is followed to fill all the gaps.

citations.claim: For tweets, the paper applies tokenization, stopword removal, and regex matching to remove special characters.
citations.quote:
[s3-p1] Tweets consists of many acronyms, emoticons and unnecessary data like pictures and URL's. So
tweets are preprocessed to represent correct emotions of public. For preprocessing of tweets we
employed three stages of filtering: Tokenization, Stopwords removal and regex matching for removing
special characters.
[s3-p2] Tweets are split into individual words based on the space and irrelevant symbols like emoticons
are removed. We form a list of individual words for each tweet.
[s3-p3] Words that do not express any emotion are called Stopwords. After splitting a tweet, words like
a,is, the, with etc. are removed from the list of words.

classification problem. The total positive, negative and neutral emotions in tweets in a 3 day period are

[s0-p1] In this work, we present a semi-supervised QA system which requires the end user to specify a

citations.quote:
Methodology
[s2-p0] Our system comprises of following three steps:
[s2-p1] Cloze generation: Most of the documents typically follow a template, they begin with an
introduction that provides an overview and a brief summary for what is to follow. We assume such a
structure while constructing our cloze style questions. When there is no clear demarcation, we treat the
first $K\%$ (hyperparameter, in our case 20%) of the document as the introduction. While noisy, this
heuristic generates a large number of clozes given any corpus, which we found to be beneficial for
semi-supervised learning despite the noise.
[s2-p2] We use a standard NLP pipeline based on Stanford CoreNLP (for SQuAD, TrivaQA and PubMed)
and the BANNER Named Entity Recognizer (only for PubMed articles) to identify entities and phrases.

discussed in detail in the remainder of the article. In effect, the cloze question from the introduction and
the matching paragraph in the body forms a question and context passage pair. We create two cloze
datasets, one each from Wikipedia corpus (for SQuAD and TriviaQA) and PUBMed academic papers (for
the BioASQ challenge), consisting of 2.2M and 1M clozes respectively. From analyzing the cloze data
manually, we were able to answer 76% times for the Wikipedia set and 80% times for the PUBMed set
using the information in the passage. In most cases the cloze paraphrased the information in the
passage, which we hypothesized to be a useful signal for the downstream QA task.

citations.claim: Pre-training QA models with automatically constructed cloze questions improves performance, especially when there are few labeled examples.
citations.quote:
Conclusion
[s6-p0] In this paper, we show that pre-training QA models with automatically constructed cloze questions
improves the performance of the models significantly, especially when there are few labeled examples.
The performance of the model trained only on the cloze questions is poor, validating the need for
fine-tuning. Through regression analysis, we find that pretraining helps with questions which ask for
factual information located in a specific part of the context. For future work, we plan to explore the active
learning setup for this task – specifically, which passages and / or types of questions can we select to
annotate, such that there is a maximum performance gain from fine-tuning. We also want to explore how
to adapt cloze style pre-training to NLP tasks other than QA.

as the structured input and the task is to generate the first sentence of the article (which typically is a
one-line description of the person). We used the same train, valid and test sets which were made publicly
available by lebret2016neural.

citations.claim: WikiBio contains around 700K infobox–description pairs and a vocabulary of around 400K words.

description} pairs and has a vocabulary of around 400K words. We show that the proposed model gives a
relative improvement of 21% and 20% as compared to current state of the art models BIBREF0 ,
BIBREF9 on this dataset. The proposed model also gives a relative improvement of 10% as compared to
the basic seq2seq model. Further, we introduce new datasets for French and German on the same lines
as the English WikiBio dataset. Even on these two datasets, our model outperforms the state of the art
methods mentioned above.
Related work

citations.claim: The authors introduce two new biography datasets, one in French and one in German.

[s6-p1] We also introduce two new biography datasets, one in French and one in German. These

(10%) and valid (10%). The French and German datasets extracted by us has been made publicly
available. The number of examples was 170K and 50K and the vocabulary size was 297K and 143K for
French and German respectively. Although in this work we focus only on generating descriptions in one
language, we hope that this dataset will also be useful for developing models which jointly learn to
generate descriptions from structured data in multiple languages.

focus is toward the latter. Given the differences between the training, development, and test sets, we
focus on methods for generalising our models. We note that propaganda identification is, in general, an
imbalanced binary classification problem as most sentences are not propagandistic.

output.answer: Salience: frequency, position, grammatical function/internal structure (POS tags, head nouns), and relative entity frequency (paragraph coverage plus positional decay). Relative authority: comparative a priori authority among co-occurring entities, where a priori authority is corpus occurrence probability or PageRank centrality and relative authority is the proportion of co-occurring entities with higher authority. Separate feature groups, combined in the model.

[s1-p5] Entity Salience. Determining which entities are prominent or salient in a given text has a long
history in NLP, sparked by the linguistic theory of Centering BIBREF14 . Salience has been used in
pronoun and co-reference resolution BIBREF15 , or to predict which entities will be included in an
abstract of an article BIBREF11 . Frequent features to measure salience include the frequency of an
entity in a document, positioning of an entity, grammatical function or internal entity structure (POS tags,
head nouns etc.). These approaches are not currently aimed at knowledge base generation or Wikipedia
coverage extension but we postulate that an entity's salience in a news article is a prerequisite to the
news article being relevant enough to be included in an entity page. We therefore use the salience
features in BIBREF11 as part of our model. However, these features are document-inte

citations.quote:
[s5-p5] Baseline Features. As discussed in Section SECREF2 , a variety of features that measure
salience of an entity in text are available from the NLP community. We reimplemented the ones in
Dunietz and Gillick BIBREF11 . This includes a variety of features, e.g. positional features, occurrence
frequency and the internal POS structure of the entity and the sentence it occurs in. Table 2 in BIBREF11
gives details.

citations.claim: The first-stage model uses entity salience, relative authority, and article novelty as separate criteria.
citations.quote:
[s0-p5] Approach and Contributions. We propose a two-stage news suggestion approach to entity pages.
In the first stage, we determine whether a news article should be suggested for an entity, based on the
entity's salience in the news article, its relative authority and the novelty of the article to the entity page.
The second stage takes into account the class of the entity for which the news is suggested and
constructs section templates from entities of the same class. The generation of such templates has the
advantage of suggesting and expanding entity pages that do not have a complete section structure in
Wikipedia, explicitly addressing long-tail and trunk entities. Afterwards, based on the constructed
template our method determines the best fit for the news article with one of the sections.

citations.claim: The paper introduces features encoding entity salience, relative authority, and novelty.
citations.quote:
[s4-p1] In the following, we describe the process of learning the functions INLINEFORM0 and
INLINEFORM1 . We introduce features for the learning process, which encode information regarding the
entity salience, relative authority and novelty in the case of AEP task. For the ASP task, we measure the
overall fit of an article to the entity sections, with the entity being an input from AEP task. Additionally,
considering that the entity profiles INLINEFORM2 are incomplete, in the case of a missing section we
suggest and expand the entity profiles based on section templates generated from entities of the same
class INLINEFORM3 (see Section UID34 ).

citations.claim: Authority and novelty are distinct feature groups that add further precision.
citations.quote:
[s5-p29] In Figure FIGREF60 we show the impact of the individual feature groups that contribute to the
superior performance in comparison to the baselines. Relative entity frequency from the salience feature,
models the entity salience as an exponentially decaying function based on the positional index of the
paragraph where the entity appears. The performance of INLINEFORM0 with relative entity frequency
from the salience feature group is close to that of all the features combined. The authority and novelty
features account to a further improvement in terms of precision, by adding roughly a 7%-10% increase.
However, if both feature groups are considered separately, they significantly outperform the baseline B1.

output.explanation: Source_1 defines generalization as performance on patients absent from training and states that the held-out set contains exactly 100 unique patients, with split assignment required by patient identifier before feature fitting. Source_2 reports that exactly 11 held-out patient identifiers also occur in training, that the remaining held-out patients do not occur in training, and that no per-patient predictions were retained. Source_3 reports an aggregate held-out accuracy of 86%, but also says feature normalization was fitted on the union of training and held-out records before the split and that only the aggregate score is available. Using source_1's denominator of 100 and source_2's overlap count of 11, contamination is 11/100 = 11%. Because 11 held-out patients were in training and preprocessing used held-out records, the 86% figure is not a clean unseen-patient estimate. The documents are complementary rather than conflicting: source_1 gives the protocol, source_2 gives the overlap audit, and source_3 gives the reported score and preprocessing leak; none supplies a corrected score. A corrected score cannot be derived from the aggregate alone because only the aggregate score is available and no per-patient predictions were retained. The minimal valid rerun is patient-level: assign the split by patient identifier before any feature fitting, fit normalization using training records only, and evaluate on held-out patients absent from training.

citations.claim: MIIB is a major myosin-II isoform that is strongly polarized in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells and is downregulated in differentiated cells via asymmetric division.
citations.quote:
[1] Here, mass spectrometry-calibrated intracellular flow cytometry of human hematopoiesis reveals MIIB
to be a major isoform that is strongly polarized in hematopoietic stem cells and progenitors (HSC/Ps) and
thereby downregulated in differentiated cells via asymmetric division.
[2] MIIA is constitutive and activated by dephosphorylation during cytokine-triggered differentiation of
cells grown on stiff, endosteum-like matrix, but not soft, marrow-like matrix.
[3] In vivo, MIIB is required for generation of blood, while MIIA is required for sustained HSC/P
engraftment.
[4] Reversible inhibition of both isoforms in culture with blebbistatin enriches for long-term hematopoietic
multilineage reconstituting cells by 5-fold or more as assessed in vivo.
[5] Megakaryocytes also become more polyploid, producing 4-fold more platelets.

Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1904.07904
Mitigating the Impact of Speech Recognition Errors on Spoken
Question Answering by Adversarial Domain Adaptation
Abstract
Spoken question answering (SQA) is challenging due to complex reasoning on top of the spoken
documents. The recent studies have also shown the catastrophic impact of automatic speech
recognition (ASR) errors on SQA. Therefore, this work proposes to mitigate the ASR errors by aligning
the mismatch between ASR hypotheses and their corresponding reference transcriptions. An
adversarial model is applied to this domain adaptation task, which forces the model to learn
domain-invariant features the QA model can effectively utilize in order to improve the SQA results. The
experiments successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed model, and the results are
better than the previous best model by 2% EM score.

CSAT dataset consists of US English telephone speech from call centers. For each call in this dataset,
customers participated in that call gave a rating on his experience with agent. Originally, this dataset
has labels rated on a scale 1-9 with 9 being extremely satisfied and 1 being extremely dissatisfied. Fig.
FIGREF16 shows the histogram of ratings for our dataset. As the distribution is skewed towards
extremes, we choose to do binary classification with ratings above 4.5 as satisfied and below 4.5 as
dissatisfied. Quantization of ratings also helped us to create a balanced dataset. This dataset contains
4331 calls and we split them into 3 sets for our experiments: 2866 calls for training, 362 calls for
validation and, finally, 1103 calls for testing.

citations.claim: The paper's model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts collected across diverse conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing.
citations.quote:
We explore linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media and construct statistical
models that can identify dogmatic comments. Our model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts, collected
across a diverse set of conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing. We operationalize
key aspects of dogmatism described by existing psychology theories (such as over-confidence), finding
they have predictive power. We also find evidence for new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency
of dogmatic posts to refrain from signaling cognitive processes. When we use our predictive model to
analyze millions of other Reddit posts, we find evidence that suggests dogmatism is a deeper
personality trait, present for dogmatic users across many different domains, and that users who engage
on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves.

Selected passages
We compare the predictions of logistic regression models based on unigram bag-of-words features
(BOW), sentiment signals (SENT), the linguistic features from our earlier analyses (LING), and
combinations of these features. BOW and SENT provide baselines for the task. We compute BOW
features using term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and category-based features by
normalizing counts for each category by the number of words in each document. The BOW classifiers

best validation performance.

Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Selected passages
To the best of our knowledge only one previous work in extractive summarization has explicitly
leveraged section information to guide the generation of summaries BIBREF5 . However, the only
information about sections fed into their sentence classifier is a categorical feature with values like
Highlight, Abstract, Introduction, etc., depending on which section the sentence appears in.
In contrast, in order to exploit section information, in this paper we propose to capture a distributed
representation of both the global (the whole document) and the local context (e.g., the section/topic)
when deciding if a sentence should be included in the summary

citations.claim: The paper proposes a neural single-document extractive summarization model for long documents.
citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1909.08089
Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a novel neural single document extractive summarization model for long
documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it
outperforms previous work, both extractive and abstractive models, on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and
METEOR scores. We also show that, consistently with our goal, the benefits of our method become
stronger as we apply it to longer documents. Rather surprisingly, an ablation study indicates that the
benefits of our model seem to come exclusively from modeling the local context, even for the longest
documents.

output.explanation: In 1512.03385v1.pdf, the ILSVRC’15 entry is an ensemble: the authors combine six models of different depth (only two 152-layer ones at submission) and report 3.57% top-5 error on the test set, winning ILSVRC 2015 [S:154860ab87fe#62]. Table 5 likewise labels the 3.57% ResNet result as an ensemble error on the ImageNet test set reported by the test server [S:154860ab87fe#53]. In 1608.06993v5.pdf, Table 3 reports DenseNet-201 at 22.58/21.46 top-1 and 6.34/5.54 top-5 for single-crop/10-crop testing, explicitly on the ImageNet validation set [S:63d1b0f26659#48]. The DenseNet ImageNet setup uses ILSVRC 2012 (1.2M training, 50k validation, 1,000 classes), 224x224 single- or 10-crop testing, and reports validation errors [S:63d1b0f26659#46]. The DenseNet authors say they replaced ResNet with DenseNet-BC while keeping all ResNet experiment settings exactly the same, and report single-crop and 10-crop validation errors [S:63d1b0f26659#66]; they also note their hyperparameters were optimized for ResNets, not DenseNets [S:63d1b0f26659#67]. The DenseNet paper further states a DenseNet-201 with 20M parameters yields similar validation error to a 101-layer ResNet with more than 40M parameters [S:63d1b0f26659#66]. Thus the 3.57% ResNet figure is an ensemble/test result, while the DenseNet-201 figures are single-model/validation results with separate single- and 10-crop values. The ResNet paper separately reports a 4.49% single-model top-5 validation error, but that is not the ILSVRC’15 ensemble number in the question [S:154860ab87fe#62]. These reported numbers therefore cannot establish a like-for-like head-to-head advantage: they differ in model count and data split, and the cited ResNet ensemble entry is not shown to use the same single-/10-crop validation protocol as DenseNet-201.

citations.claim: DeiT’s class token is a trainable vector appended to the patch tokens before the first layer and projected with a linear layer to predict the class.
citations.quote:
The class token
is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the
ﬁrst layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with
a linear layer to predict the class. This class token is inherited from NLP [14],
and departs from the typical pooling layers used in computer vision to predict
the class. The transformer thus process batches of (N + 1) tokens of dimension
D, of which only the class vector is used to predict the output. This architecture
forces the self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and
the class token: at training time the supervision signal comes only from the
class embedding, while the patch tokens are the model’s only variable input.

output.explanation: ViT states that a learnable [class] embedding is prepended to the patch embeddings and that its output state serves as the image representation with a classification head attached [S:09514e334c4e#19]. ViT also says the [class] token is taken as the image representation and its output is transformed into a class prediction by a small tanh-MLP [S:09514e334c4e#117]. DeiT describes the class token as a trainable vector appended before the first transformer layer and projected by a linear layer to predict the class [S:3efc0a7acf39#23]. For distillation, DeiT says the distillation token is used similarly to the class token except that its objective is to reproduce the teacher’s hard label instead of the true label; both tokens are learned by back-propagation [S:3efc0a7acf39#28]. At inference, DeiT associates both the class and distillation embeddings with linear classifiers and, for late fusion, adds the softmax outputs of the two classifiers to make the prediction [S:3efc0a7acf39#33]. The papers agree that the class token supplies the image-level representation used for classification; DeiT differs by adding a distillation token and by using a linear classifier rather than an MLP head for pre-training [S:3efc0a7acf39#34]. Limitation: the statement that the class branch is trained by the true label is inferred from DeiT’s contrast that the distillation token reproduces the teacher’s hard label “instead of true label”; no separate sentence explicitly names the class-branch target.

validation and, finally, 1103 calls for testing.

citations.claim: The paper constructs statistical models to identify dogmatic comments from linguistic and behavioral features.
citations.quote:
We explore linguistic and behavioral features of dogmatism in social media and construct statistical
models that can identify dogmatic comments. Our model is based on a corpus of Reddit posts, collected
across a diverse set of conversational topics and annotated via paid crowdsourcing. We operationalize
key aspects of dogmatism described by existing psychology theories (such as over-confidence), finding
they have predictive power. We also find evidence for new signals of dogmatism, such as the tendency
of dogmatic posts to refrain from signaling cognitive processes. When we use our predictive model to
analyze millions of other Reddit posts, we find evidence that suggests dogmatism is a deeper
personality trait, present for dogmatic users across many different domains, and that users who engage
on dogmatic comments tend to show increases in dogmatic posts themselves.

citations.quote:
We introduce a new task called Multimodal Named Entity Recognition (MNER) for noisy user-generated
data such as tweets or Snapchat captions, which comprise short text with accompanying images. These
social media posts often come in inconsistent or incomplete syntax and lexical notations with very
limited surrounding textual contexts, bringing significant challenges for NER. To this end, we create a
new dataset for MNER called SnapCaptions (Snapchat image-caption pairs submitted to public and
crowd-sourced stories with fully annotated named entities). We then build upon the state-of-the-art
Bi-LSTM word/character based NER models with 1) a deep image network which incorporates relevant
visual context to augment textual information, and 2) a generic modality-attention module which learns
to attenuate irrelevant modalities while amplifying the most informative ones to extract contexts from,

citations.quote:
Research extract  /  QASPER dev  /  arXiv 1909.08089
Extractive Summarization of Long Documents by Combining
Global and Local Context
Abstract
In this paper, we propose a novel neural single document extractive summarization model for long
documents, incorporating both the global context of the whole document and the local context within the
current topic. We evaluate the model on two datasets of scientific papers, Pubmed and arXiv, where it
outperforms previous work, both extractive and abstractive models, on ROUGE-1, ROUGE-2 and
METEOR scores. We also show that, consistently with our goal, the benefits of our method become
stronger as we apply it to longer documents. Rather surprisingly, an ablation study indicates that the
benefits of our model seem to come exclusively from modeling the local context, even for the longest
documents.

citations.claim: DeiT describes the class token as a trainable vector appended to patch tokens before the first transformer layer.
citations.quote:
The class token
is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the
ﬁrst layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with
a linear layer to predict the class. This class token is inherited from NLP [14],
and departs from the typical pooling layers used in computer vision to predict
the class. The transformer thus process batches of (N + 1) tokens of dimension
D, of which only the class vector is used to predict the output. This architecture
forces the self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and
the class token: at training time the supervision signal comes only from the
class embedding, while the patch tokens are the model’s only variable input.
5

Figure 2: Our distillation procedure: we simply include a new distillation token.
It interacts with the class and patch tokens through the self-attention layers.
This distillation token is employed in a similar fashion as the class token, ex-
cept that on output of the network its objective is to reproduce the (hard) label
predicted by the teacher, instead of true label. Both the class and distillation

output.explanation: ViT (2010.11929v2.pdf) and DeiT (2012.12877v2.pdf) agree that the class token is the image-level representation used for classification: ViT calls the extra [class] token the image representation and maps its output to a class prediction [S:09514e334c4e#117], while DeiT calls it a trainable vector that goes through the transformer layers and is projected to the class [S:3efc0a7acf39#23]. DeiT contrasts the distillation token with the class token: the distillation token is trained to reproduce the teacher's hard predicted label 'instead of true label' [S:3efc0a7acf39#28], so the class branch is the true-label branch. At test time, both embeddings have separate linear classifiers, and the referent late fusion adds the two softmax outputs [S:3efc0a7acf39#33]; Table 3 labels the class+distillation result as this late fusion [S:3efc0a7acf39#40]. The papers do not conflict on the class-token role; DeiT says its architecture is identical to ViT with no convolutions and differs in training strategies and the distillation token [S:3efc0a7acf39#34]. On the classification head, ViT's appendix describes a small MLP with tanh [S:09514e334c4e#117], whereas DeiT says it uses a linear classifier rather than an MLP head for pre-training [S:3efc0a7acf39#34]; this is a head/training detail, not a disagreement about the token's role.
